Thus every weak-norm pairing vanishes. Since the inclusion of the
strong completion into the weak completion is injective, $h=0$.
The argument uses transverse regularity of the strong space; it asserts

replacements.after:
Apply the same argument to each fixed smooth test with its finite
$C^p$ norm, and then use density in the little-$C^q$ norm. It follows
that every $C^q$ stable-curve pairing vanishes, not only the weak
$C^p$ pairings. Thus all the coordinates defining $\|h\|_s$ vanish.
Each coordinate defining $\|h\|_u$ is a scaled difference of two
$C^p$ stable pairings, so these coordinates vanish as well.

Here this conclusion is also valid on the completion. Map a smooth
density to the collection of its normalized stable pairings and
normalized differences in \eqref{eq:v35-stable-norm} and
\eqref{eq:v35-unstable-norm}. This is an isometric embedding into the
product of the two corresponding spaces of bounded coordinate
families, with the sum norm. A strong Cauchy sequence converges
uniformly in these coordinates. The extension to the completion is
therefore isometric onto the closure of its range. All the limiting
coordinates of $h$ have just been shown to vanish, whence
$\|h\|_s+c_0\|h\|_u=0$ and $h=0$. No injective map into the weak
completion is assumed in this inference. The argument uses transverse
regularity of the strong space and says nothing analogous about the
entire weak completion.

replacements.before: We impose the following geometric conditions.
replacements.after:
We impose the following conditions, separated precisely as
\textup{(H1)--(H7)} in Section~\ref{sec:v36-family-inputs}. In particular
finite-cover mixing is an independent dynamical input, verified for
our concrete tables by Proposition~\ref{prop:v36-cover-mixing}; it is
not an inference from connectedness alone.

replacements.before:
The free
region in every finite lattice cover is connected. Thus the unforced
collision theory in \cite{DZ11,DZ,Young} applies locally in parameter,
including its homogeneous curve estimates, product rectangles,
compact embedding and mixing of each finite-cover collision map.
These are the unweighted dynamical inputs to the principle.
replacements.after:
The unforced collision theory provides local common strong and weak
spaces, uniform geometric sums and a common-space spectral splitting
as specified in \textup{(H2)}. The action and matched-curve assumptions
are \textup{(H4)}. We separately assume mixing of the collision map on
each finite lattice cover, as in \textup{(H3)}. This last assertion is
qualitative for each cover: no mixing rate uniform in its degree is
required. The common-space statement is local in parameter; a finite
cover of the compact parameter space is used, not a single global
Banach space.

replacements.before:
The family \eqref{eq:v35-ellipses} satisfies all three geometric
conditions above.
replacements.after:
The family \eqref{eq:v35-ellipses} satisfies the separated conditions
\textup{(H1)--(H7)}, and hence the conditions of the preceding theorem.

replacements.before:
The positive gaps give a
connected free region in every finite lattice cover. These covers are
ordinary finite-horizon dispersing billiards with finitely many
strictly convex smooth obstacles; the mixing and local product
construction of \cite[Section 8, Theorem 6]{Young} apply to each.
One may take a rectangular Euclidean cover of the triangular torus;
no affine change of Euclidean reflection is used.
replacements.after:
The positive gaps give a connected free region in every finite
lattice cover. Mixing is supplied separately by
Proposition~\ref{prop:v36-cover-mixing}, which applies
\cite[Section 8.1, Theorem 6(b)]{Young} to the collision map of each
cover and extends its correlation conclusion to $L^2$. In particular
it excludes a nontrivial finite cyclic component of the map, not just
of the flow. No rate uniform in the number of sheets is used.
The coverings retain the Euclidean metric and reflection law.
